newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan remains richest in overseas assets.
newsitem.headline: Japan remains richest in overseas assets.

text.p: Japan has retained its position as the richest nation in terms of foreign investments for the sixth consecutive year, surpassing second-place Germany by about 86 trillion yen ($747 billion), according to a government report.

The finance Ministry report, released late on Friday, said Japan's external assets balance -- total assets held by government and businesses abroad minus liabilities -- rose by 22.9 percent from a year earlier to a record 103.36 trillion yen ($898 billion) at the end of 1996.
The report said Germany's foreign assets were 17.58 trillion yen ($152 billion) as of the end of June 1996. It did not give the figure for the end of 1996.

The finance ministry attributed the rise to a sharp growth of investment in foreign bonds due to the wide interest rate gap between Japan and overseas, and on the increase in the yen value of foreign investments because of the depreciation of the yen.

Investment in foreign securities increased to 108.71 trillion yen ($945 billion), up from 88.26 trillion yen ($767 billion) at the end of 1995 because of active buying by institutional and individual investors last year, the ministry said.
The yen 's exchange rate used for the report was 115.98 yen to the dollar, compared with 102.91 yen a year earlier.

The growth rate in the net external assets in 1996 was the second highest since 1992, though still below the high level of over 30 percent a year in the asset-inflated "bubble economy" era of the late 1980s, it said.

The ratio of Japan's net external assets to gross domestic product was 20.7 percent at the end of last year, the highest since 1972, indicating that Japan was taking its earnings from exports and investing them overseas.
Britain and France were the other net creditors among the remaining Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations, while Canada, Italy and the United States showed net deficits, the report said.

Japanese direct investments such as purchases of real estate and construction of factories abroad increased by 22.3 percent to 30 billion yen ($260 million), reflecting the continuing shift towards offshore production by Japanese manufacturers, it said.

On the other hand, the balance of Japan's external debts at the end of 1996 marked 204.34 trillion yen ($1.77 trillion), up 9.5 percent from a year before, mostly from an increase in investments by foreigners into the relatively cheaper Japanese stock market, it said.
